tracks.title: Interview in two weeks
tracks.audience: You have an interview soon and want the highest-yield route.
tracks.summary: Learn the method first, then the most-asked designs, then drill. The time shown counts reading only; add practice sessions.

steps.why: Learn the 45-minute script and the scoring rubric before you read any design. You will return to it at the end for three timed mock sessions.
Estimation is step 2 of every answer. Learn the latency numbers and the method.
A warm-up with caching, key generation and the 301 versus 302 trade-off.
Unique ID generation: the Snowflake layout, ticket servers, UUIDv7 and what happens when a clock moves backwards. Key generation comes up inside many designs.
Rate limiting, and the fail-open versus fail-closed choice (Stripe fails open; Envoy lets you choose).
Replication, quorums and consistent hashing, which recur everywhere.
Caching in depth: stale sets, stampedes and what happens when a cache server dies.
Real-time messaging, delivery guarantees and fan-out.
Fan-out on write versus read, the classic feed question.
Queues, priorities, retries and deduplication.
The message log in depth: partitions, replication, consumer groups and leader failover (Kafka), the engine under many queue answers.
Upload, transcoding and delivery of video.
Geospatial indexing and matching.
Idempotency and correctness with money.
Contention and double-booking.
Sagas and the outbox: the standard answer to cross-service consistency.
SLOs, error budgets and how to stop a cascading failure.
Estimation drills with worked solutions, so the arithmetic is automatic.
Practise spotting flaws in plausible designs. Some scenarios draw on incidents (C01 to C03) and AI notes outside this track; skip those or read them first.
Flashcards for the AI systems (22 to 31), the primers and the incident casebook. They add facts beyond the systems above rather than repeating them.
Open scenarios that practise stating a decision and its trade-offs. Finish by running three timed mock sessions from the first step.

tracks.title: Building blocks first
tracks.audience: You are earlier in your career, or want solid foundations before full designs.
tracks.summary: The small pieces that appear inside every large design: IDs, caches, locks, counters, storage engines, load balancers and APIs.

steps.why: Start with how to estimate, so every later design has numbers.
The simplest building block: unique IDs, and what happens when clocks go wrong.
Your first complete design, built from IDs and caches.
Counters, windows and failure modes in a small system.
How data is partitioned and replicated across machines.
B-trees, LSM trees and how to choose a database.
Caching at large scale.
Leader election, locks and fencing.
Top-K, approximate counting and leaderboards.
How traffic is spread across servers.
Pagination, idempotency and evolving APIs.
Consistency across services.

tracks.title: Senior engineer to architect
tracks.audience: You design well already and want the decision-making, risk and communication side.
tracks.summary: Records of decisions, deployment shape, real failures, migrations, disaster recovery, multi-tenancy, security, reliability and cost, then exercises that ask for a justified decision.

steps.why: How architects decide, record and defend decisions: ADRs, design docs and boring technology.
A deployment process that bypassed staging: read the incident, then write your own safeguards.
Automated failover meeting split writes: availability versus integrity.
Reliability as a design input: SLOs, error budgets and postmortems.
Replacing parts of a running system safely.
Monolith or microservices: the premium Fowler describes, Shopify's modular monolith, Prime Video's consolidation of one service, and Conway's law.
Threat modeling and zero trust at design time.
What drives cost and how to talk about it.
Multi-tenancy: isolation is not authentication, silo versus pool, and the noisy-neighbour mitigations. Cost and limits per tenant follow from the cost primer.
A control plane and data plane at scale, with steering.
A design where correctness dominates everything else.
Event sourcing and CQRS: when a history of changes is worth the cost, what it does to consistency, and the lighter alternatives. Compare with how payments get correctness from idempotency.
The shared coordination service many systems depend on, and its risks.
A routine operation with too much blast radius.
Recovery tools that depend on the thing that failed.
RTO, RPO and the four disaster-recovery strategies, and why recovery that depends on the failing system, or is never rehearsed, does not work.
Deployment verification, dead code and kill switches.
Hidden resource limits and dependency cascades.
Six open scenarios: write the decision record, then compare with what a strong answer covers.
Review flawed designs the way a design review would.

tracks.title: AI systems engineer
tracks.audience: You build or operate LLM-based products and want to design them well.
tracks.summary: Serving, retrieval, agents, improving models and training, followed by the security and cost questions every AI feature raises.

steps.why: How LLMs are served: KV cache, batching and the prefill/decode split.
Vector search: the indexes behind retrieval.
Retrieval-augmented generation as a system: chunking, hybrid search, permissions.
Agents: workflows versus loops, tools, sandboxes and budgets.
Improving a model: adapters, preference tuning, evaluation gates and rollout.
Two-stage recommendation and learning from feedback.
Training at scale: parallelism, checkpoints and failure.
Threat modeling, which matters most for tools and retrieved text.
Tokens and GPU hours as the cost drivers.
Scenario 6 asks for an AI feature design with safety and evaluation.

tracks.title: The whole atlas in learning order
tracks.audience: You want to study systematically over several weeks.
tracks.summary: All 35 systems, from foundations to AI, in the order the stages build on each other.
